newsitem.title: UK: Blair woos Clinton with UK cabinet meeting invite.
newsitem.headline: Blair woos Clinton with UK cabinet meeting invite.

text.p: Britain's new Prime Minister Tony Blair will seek to get off on the right foot with the U.S. administration this week by granting President Bill Clinton the unprecedented honour of attending a meeting of his cabinet.
The move will emphasise the readiness of Blair, whose Labour Party won a landslide victory in Britain's May 1 election, to seek advice from all quarters on his conduct of foreign policy.

A spokesman in his office on Sunday confirmed newspaper reports that Blair held a meeting for almost an hour last Thursday with Margaret Thatcher, a figure reviled by Labour during her her 11 years as Conservative Prime Minister.

Clinton is coming to London next Thursday after two days in continental Europe attending a NATO-Russian summit and marking the 50th anniversary of the Marshall Plan which helped Europe's economies revive after World War Two.
British government sources said newspaper reports that Clinton would become the first foreign outsider formally to address the 22-member cabinet exaggerated the position.
"There will be a cabinet (meeting). He will meet the cabinet and he is expected to say a few words," one source said.
But even the modest ceremony planned by the White House and Blair's Downing Street office breaks all precedents, and indicates the close political sympathies between the two men.
Both have pulled their countries towards the centre ground of politics by defeating political forces to their right.

"He (Blair) and Clinton get on extremely well. They have got a very good personal relationship. They have a very keen mutual interest in certain issues such as education and welfare reform," a Blair aide told journalists last week.
The government sources confirmed that while their husbands hold talks on Thursday, Clinton's wife Hillary will have lunch with Cherie Blair, a high-flying lawyer.

Clinton was the first world leader to congratulate Blair on his stunning election victory, phoning him in his car as it sped towards London from his northern England Sedgefield constituency in the early hours of May 2.

Some British newspapers speculated that Clinton was pleased to see the back of John Major's Conservatives, who supported Republican President George Bush against him in the 1992 U.S. Presidential race.
In the 3-1/2 weeks it has been in office, Blair's government has charted a new path for British diplomacy.

Blair was in the Dutch town of Noordwijk on Friday to meet fellow European leaders who greeted his election as a chance to end the prickly relations which existed between Britain and its EU partners under Thatcher and Major.
The Downing Street spokesman declined to discuss what topics Thatcher and Blair discussed at their meeting last week.
But British media speculated that U.S. relations must have been one given that Thatcher got on very well with then U.S. President Ronald Reagan when she was in office.
"There have been occasions in the past when Prime Ministers have invited predecessors of different parties in for talks," said the spokesman, playing down the significance of the visit.
